text:
[Atrial Fibrillation | Cardiology | ICD-10 I48.91 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.12]
clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Rapid rate palpitations
  - General fatigue, weakness or exhaustion
  - Dizziness, near syncope or syncope
  - Shortness of breath
  - Chest pain
  - Symptoms more marked on exertion
Signs:
  - Irregularly irregular pulse
  - Variable heart sound
Risk factors:
  - Prior valvular heart disease, CHF or MI
  - Prior TIA, stroke or embolic episode
  - Hypertension
  - Diabetes mellitus
  - COPD
  - CKD
  - Obesity
Precipitating factors:
  - Post cardiac surgery
  - Alcoholism or binge drinking
  - Myo-pericarditis or acute coronary syndrome
  - Pneumonitis or pulmonary embolism
  - Sepsis
  - Hyperthyroidism
Red flags:
  - Systolic BP 90 mmHg
  - Heart rate greater than 150/min or less than 50/min
  - Ongoing angina
  - CHF, TIA or stroke
  - Major bleed on oral anticoagulants

text:
[Atrial Fibrillation | Cardiology | ICD-10 I48.91 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.12]
care_level:
Phc chc:
  - Detailed clinical evaluation
  - Basic investigations
  - Careful ECG evaluation
  - Start oral anticoagulation if indicated based on stroke risk
  - Start Metoprolol if HR greater than 110/min and no evidence of CHF
  - Refer if indicators for early intervention
District:
  - Admit if indicators of early intervention
  - Immediate cardioversion after heparinization if hemodynamic instability
  - Manage precipitating factors
  - Assess stroke, bleeding risk and coagulation parameters
  - Detailed echocardiogram
  - Start OAC, maintain INR around 2-3
  - Control HR by single drug or combination of beta blocker and calcium channel blocker
Tertiary:
  - Re-assess clinical status and adequacy of anticoagulation
  - Consider need of NOAC
  - Optimise management of underlying cardiac disease
  - Stress lifestyle and AF risk factor modification
  - Assess need for rhythm control and discuss pros and cons
  - Consider radiofrequency ablation in select patients

[Atrial Fibrillation | Cardiology | ICD-10 I48.91 | procedure | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.12]
procedures:
-
  Name: Direct current cardioversion
  Required level: District hospital or above
  Indications:
    - Hemodynamic instability
    - Very rapid HR greater than 130/min not controlled
    - HR remains greater than 110/min after rate control attempt
  Prerequisites:     - Heparinization before cardioversion in hemodynamic instability
-
  Name: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
  Required level: Tertiary centre
  Indications:     - Select patients after assessment of need for rhythm control and discussion of pros and cons
  Note: Keep a high threshold for invasive procedures
-
  Name: Conversion to normal sinus rhythm
  Required level: District or tertiary
  Indications:
    - Hemodynamic instability
    - Uncontrolled symptoms despite heart rate control
    - Unacceptable rate control drug side effects
    - Patient preference

text:
[Bradyarrhythmias in Symptomatic Patients | Cardiology | ICD-10 R00.1 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.13]
clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Syncope, presyncope or dizziness
  - Lethargy or fatigue
  - Breathlessness or chest pain on exertion
Entry rule: Any of the listed symptoms AND persistent pulse rate less than 50 bpm
History:
  - Syncope/presyncope frequency, associated fall, injury or incontinence
  - Exertional angina or known coronary artery disease
  - Known hypothyroidism or kidney disease
  - On beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers or digoxin
  - Patient with an implanted pacemaker or other device
  - Yellow oleander poisoning
Red flags:
  - Hypotension (SBP less than 90 mmHg), impaired consciousness or ongoing chest pain
  - Recurrent or ongoing syncope/presyncope
  - Associated headache with or without neurologic deficit (suspect intracranial event)
  - Patient with a pre-existing device
  - ECG showing complete heart block
  - Sinus node disease with pauses greater than 3 seconds
  - Bradycardia HR less than 50 bpm with or without hyperkalemia (serum K greater than 5 mEq/L)

text:
[Bradyarrhythmias in Symptomatic Patients | Cardiology | ICD-10 R00.1 | procedure | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.13]
procedures:
-
  Name: Temporary pacemaker insertion
  Required level: District hospital or above
  Indications:     - Unstable symptomatic bradycardia
  Bridging: IV dopamine or adrenaline may be given until TPI can be placed
-
  Name: Permanent pacing
  Required level: Tertiary centre
  Indications:
    - AV nodal disease: complete heart block, advanced AV block, or Mobitz Type II block
    - AV nodal disease: symptomatic patients with AV block other than the above
    - AV nodal disease: associated neuromuscular disease
    - Sinus node dysfunction: symptomatic patients with sinus pauses greater than 3 seconds with symptom correlation
    - Sinus node dysfunction: asymptomatic patients with sinus pauses greater than 6 seconds
    - Other conduction disorders with 1:1 AV conduction: symptomatic patients with HV interval 100 ms or more on EPS
    - Other conduction disorders: alternating bundle branch block, infiltrative or neuromuscular disease
  Modes:
    -
      Scenario: Sinus node dysfunction with intact AV conduction
      Mode: Atrial-based single or dual chamber pacing; VVI reasonable if symptoms infrequent
    -
      Scenario: AV node disease with LVEF greater than 50 percent
      Mode: VVI or dual chamber pacing
    -
      Scenario: AV node disease with LVEF 36-50 percent requiring ventricular pacing more than 40 percent of the time
      Mode: CRT or His bundle pacing
    -
      Scenario: LV dysfunction less than 35 percent
      Mode: CRT or His bundle pacing

text:
[Heart Failure (Breathless Patient) | Cardiology | ICD-10 I50.9 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.14]
clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Dyspnea, orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  - Pink frothy sputum
  - Dependent pedal edema
  - Recent weight gain
  - Easy fatiguability
  - History of CHF or MI
Signs:
  - Tachypnoea
  - Tachycardia or irregular pulse
  - Basal crepitations
  - Cardiomegaly
  - Presence of murmurs
  - Systemic desaturation
  - Raised JVP
  - Pulmonary oedema
  - Pleural effusions
  - Hepatomegaly
  - Ascites
  - Pitting oedema
Etiology:
  - Ischemic cardiomyopathy (past MI)
  - Diabetic cardiomyopathy
  - Rheumatic heart disease with existing valvular disease
  - Post-viral (acute onset breathlessness within last 3 months)
  - Peri-partum cardiomyopathy (onset in last trimester or after delivery)
  - Idiopathic cardiomyopathy
  - Post-cancer chemotherapy
Red flags:
  - BP less than 90 mmHg or greater than 200 mmHg
  - Heart rate less than 50/min or greater than 120/min
  - Respiratory rate greater than 30/min or cyanosis
  - Oliguria
  - Altered sensorium

text:
[Heart Failure (Breathless Patient) | Cardiology | ICD-10 I50.9 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.14]
care_level:
Phc chc:
  - Rule out respiratory cause
  - Likely CHF: decongest with furosemide
  - Refer if red flag criteria met
Chc:
  - Admit and stabilize
  - Routine investigations
  - ECG to rule out acute ST-elevation MI
  - Chest X-ray to rule out respiratory etiology
  - Decongest with intravenous furosemide
  - Oxygen therapy if systemic saturation less than 90 percent
  - Start enalapril and spironolactone orally
  - Consider carvedilol after decongestion
District:
  - Admit and re-assess
  - Optimise therapy with furosemide, enalapril, spironolactone, oxygen
  - Consider non-invasive ventilation if marked respiratory distress and O2 saturation less than 90 percent
  - Echocardiography to confirm HFrEF (LV ejection fraction less than 35 percent)
  - Search for etiological diagnosis
  - Consider carvedilol after decongestion
  - Refer back to CHC/PHC after stabilization
Tertiary:
  - Re-assess and confirm diagnosis
  - Categorize acute vs chronic and HFrEF vs HFpEF
  - Optimize therapy
  - Consider ARNI and ivabradine
  - Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines
  - Investigate etiology
  - Consider non-pharmacological invasive therapy
  - Etiology based interventions
text_for_display:
care_level:
Phc chc:
  - Rule out respiratory cause
  - Likely CHF: decongest with furosemide
  - Refer if red flag criteria met
Chc:
  - Admit and stabilize
  - Routine investigations
  - ECG to rule out acute ST-elevation MI
  - Chest X-ray to rule out respiratory etiology
  - Decongest with intravenous furosemide
  - Oxygen therapy if systemic saturation less than 90 percent
  - Start enalapril and spironolactone orally
  - Consider carvedilol after decongestion
District:
  - Admit and re-assess
  - Optimise therapy with furosemide, enalapril, spironolactone, oxygen
  - Consider non-invasive ventilation if marked respiratory distress and O2 saturation less than 90 percent
  - Echocardiography to confirm HFrEF (LV ejection fraction less than 35 percent)
  - Search for etiological diagnosis
  - Consider carvedilol after decongestion
  - Refer back to CHC/PHC after stabilization
Tertiary:
  - Re-assess and confirm diagnosis
  - Categorize acute vs chronic and HFrEF vs HFpEF
  - Optimize therapy
  - Consider ARNI and ivabradine
  - Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines
  - Investigate etiology
  - Consider non-pharmacological invasive therapy
  - Etiology based interventions

drugs:
-
  Name: Furosemide
  Dose: 20-80 mg daily PO; intravenous 10-40 mg SOS in acute stage
  Monitoring: Serum electrolytes, creatinine and uric acid on therapy
-
  Name: Spironolactone
  Dose: 25-50 mg once daily PO
  Monitoring: Serum potassium and creatinine every 2-4 weeks
-
  Name: Enalapril
  Dose: 2.5 to 10 mg twice daily PO
  Conditions: Start low dose with BP greater than 100 mmHg, normal electrolytes and creatinine less than 2.5 mg/dl
  Monitoring: BP and electrolytes before every increment
-
  Name: Carvedilol
  Dose: 3.125 to 25 mg twice daily PO
  Conditions: Start after decongestion with low dose, BP greater than 100 mmHg and HR greater than 60/min
  Monitoring: BP, heart rate and reappearance of CHF symptoms
-
  Name: ARNI
  Indication: Tertiary level optimisation
-
  Name: Ivabradine
  Indication: Tertiary level optimisation

text:
[Stable Angina | Cardiology | ICD-10 I20.9 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.15]
clinical_criteria:
Consider angina if:
  - Diffuse retrosternal pain, heaviness or constriction radiating to arms, neck or back
  - Associated with sweating
  - Easily reproduced with post-meal exertion
  - Atypical presentation: exertional fatigue, breathlessness, profuse sweating or epigastric discomfort
Angina unlikely if:
  - Variable location or characteristic
  - Long lasting (hours to days) or short lasting (less than a minute)
  - Restricted to areas above jaw or below epigastrium
  - Localized to a point
  - Pricking, piercing or stabbing type of pain
  - Precipitated by movement of neck or arms or respiration
Escalate to acs if:
  - Angina at rest or lasting more than 20 minutes
  - Recent worsening of stable angina (crescendo) to CCS class III
  - New onset effort angina of less than 1 month in CCS class II/III
  - Post infarction angina

text:
[Stable Angina | Cardiology | ICD-10 I20.9 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.15]
care_level:
Phc chc:
  - Control angina with Metoprolol, add nitrates if symptoms not controlled
  - ECG for Q waves, ST-T changes, BBB or chamber enlargement
  - Aspirin and high intensity statins
  - Refer to higher centre electively
District:
  - Optimise anti-anginal treatment
  - Echocardiography for LV function or structural heart disease
  - Risk stratify by exercise treadmill test using DUKE risk score if patient is ambulatory and ECG is interpretable
Tertiary:
  - Reassess and optimise drug therapy; if uncontrolled choose from trimetazidine, nicorandil, ranolazine and ivabradine
  - Risk stratify with exercise treadmill test if not already done
  - Stress imaging where indicated

[Stable Angina | Cardiology | ICD-10 I20.9 | procedure | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.15]
procedures:
-
  Name: Coronary angiography
  Required level: Tertiary centre
  Indications:
    - High risk group AND angina not controlled on optimal medical therapy
    - High risk on non-invasive testing
    - Cardiac arrest survivor or documented ventricular tachycardia
-
  Name: Revascularization (PCI or CABG)
  Required level: Tertiary centre
  Indications:     - Anatomy suitable on angiography
  Rules:
    - Prefer CABG over PCI in diabetes mellitus with multivessel disease or left main disease
    - Complete re-vascularization is preferable
    - Use invasive functional and imaging modalities (FFR, IVUS, OCT) when indicated
    - Continue dual anti-platelets (aspirin and clopidogrel) after PCI
  Prerequisites:     - Discussion of pros and cons of revascularization and dual anti-platelet therapy
-
  Name: Stress imaging
  Required level: Tertiary centre
  Indications:
    - Non ambulatory patient
    - Abnormal or uninterpretable baseline ECG
    - Equivocal exercise treadmill test result
    - Compromised LV function

Elective angiography/revascularization in stable angina requires documented failure of optimal medical therapy OR high risk on non-invasive testing. text:
[ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) | Cardiology | ICD-10 I21.3 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.16]
clinical_criteria:
Acs definition:
  - Angina at rest or lasting more than 20 minutes
  - Recent worsening of stable angina (crescendo) to CCS class III
  - New onset effort angina of less than 1 month in CCS class II/III
  - Post infarction angina
Differential:
  - Pleuritis, pneumonitis, embolism, pneumothorax
  - Pericardial rub
  - Neuralgia or herpes
  - Aortic dissection (unequal or absent peripheral pulses)

text:
[ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) | Cardiology | ICD-10 I21.3 | procedure | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.16]
procedures:
-
  Name: Primary PCI
  Required level: PCI capable hospital
  Indications:     - STEMI within 12 hours where PCI achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact
  Timing targets:     - Preferably within 90 minutes; under 60 minutes in early presenters
  Intraprocedural rules:
    - Use unfractionated heparin
    - No routine thrombosuction
    - Tackle culprit artery only unless shock
    - Drug eluting stent preferred
  Post procedure:     - Continue dual antiplatelets for at least 1 year
-
  Name: Rescue PCI
  Required level: PCI capable hospital
  Indications:     - Failed fibrinolysis (less than 50 percent ST settlement or no pain relief at 60-90 minutes)
-
  Name: Routine early PCI after successful fibrinolysis
  Required level: PCI capable hospital
  Indications:     - Successful thrombolysis
  Timing targets:     - Preferably 3-24 hours
-
  Name: Thrombolysis
  Required level: Non PCI capable centre where transfer not feasible
  Indications:     - Within 12 hours of symptom onset with no contraindication
  Timing targets:     - Therapy to be started within 10 minutes preferably; within 30 minutes of diagnosis
  Agent preference: Fibrin specific agent Tenecteplase, TPA or Reteplase; Streptokinase if fibrin-specific unavailable

text:
[Unstable Angina / NSTEMI | Cardiology | ICD-10 I20.0 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.17]
care_level:
Phc chc:
  - ECG, troponin
  - Start aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin/LMWH, high dose atorvastatin, metoprolol
  - Risk stratify with GRACE or TIMI score
  - Refer high/intermediate risk to PCI capable centre; refer low risk to district hospital
  - Refer to PCI capable centre if acute LVF, hypotension, systolic murmur or arrhythmia
District:
  - Admit in ICU equipped with ECG monitoring and defibrillator
  - Troponin and biochemistry
  - Serial ECG and echocardiography
  - Continue aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin and metoprolol
  - Add nitrates if needed
  - Very high, high or intermediate risk or LVEF less than 40 percent: refer for revascularization
  - Low risk: conservative management, lifestyle modification, risk factor control, secondary prevention
Tertiary:
  - Admit, reassess and monitor in ICCU
  - Continue aspirin and heparin
  - Load with clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor if not already done
  - Optimal medical therapy
  - Detailed echocardiography
  - Low risk patients may undergo non-invasive risk stratification
  - Very high, high and intermediate risk may be subjected to coronary revascularization

text:
[Unstable Angina / NSTEMI | Cardiology | ICD-10 I20.0 | procedure | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.17]
procedures:
-
  Name: Coronary revascularization
  Required level: Tertiary / PCI capable centre
  Indications:
    - Very high, high or intermediate risk category
    - LVEF less than 40 percent
    - Low risk with recurrent pain, hemodynamic deterioration or new ECG change
  Rules:
    - Revascularize if anatomy is suitable
    - Prefer CABG over PCI in DM with multivessel disease or left main disease
    - Very high risk: urgent revascularization within a few hours after loading preferably with ticagrelor or prasugrel if PCI planned
    - Continue dual anti-platelets for at least 12 months in DES and 3 months in BMS
  Prerequisites:     - Discuss pros and cons of revascularization and prolonged dual anti-platelet therapy

medication_rules:
-
  Rule: ACEI/ARB preferred for proteinuric patients (more than 1 g/d)
  Caution: Caution or do not use if eGFR less than 30 ml/min, or potassium greater than 5.5 mEq/L
-
  Rule: Diuretic selection by eGFR
  Detail: eGFR greater than 45: thiazide; less than 45 ml/min: furosemide; less than 30 ml/min: do not use potassium sparing agents
-   Rule: Do not use metformin if eGFR less than 30
-   Rule: Do not use NSAIDs
-   Rule: Restrict green leafy vegetables if eGFR less than 30 ml/min
-   Rule: Hyperphosphatemia (PO4 greater than 5.5): start with calcium-containing binders; non-calcium binders only if serum calcium greater than 9 mg/dl, vascular calcification or low iPTH
-   Rule: Anemia: establish iron replete state; if Hb still less than 8 g/dl start erythropoietin
-   Rule: Hepatitis B vaccination if HBV negative: 20 microgram IM in each deltoid at 0, 1, 2 and 6 months

  - BP control (less than 130/80 mmHg in adults, less than 95th centile for age in children)

  - Avoid nephrotoxic agents

  - Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus)
  - Cyclophosphamide
  - Azathioprine
  - Mycophenolate mofetil
  - Levamisole
  - Rituximab

treatment_rules:
-
  Population: Cystitis/UTI in females
  Regimen: Empirical treatment, no tests needed. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BD for 5 days or TMP/SMX 1 DS tab PO BD for 3 days. If no response refer to higher centre.
  Caution: Avoid nitrofurantoin if GFR less than 45; caution in elderly
-
  Population: Male acute cystitis / simple UTI
  Regimen: Treat men for 7 days: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BD 7d, or TMP/SMX 1 DS PO BD 7d, or Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD 7 days, or Levofloxacin 750 mg OD 5 days. Acute cystitis is not to be referred.
-
  Population: All other male UTI
  Regimen: Refer: pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, pelvic or perineal pain (prostatitis)
-
  Population: Asymptomatic bacteriuria
  Regimen: No treatment required. Exceptions requiring treatment: pregnancy, before any urological intervention.
-
  Population: Catheter associated UTI
  Regimen: Treatment of asymptomatic CAUTI is NOT recommended. Remove catheters as soon as not required. If indwelling more than 2 weeks and still indicated, replace catheter. Symptomatic CAUTI (fever, back pain, new onset delirium, rigors): send culture and treat as complicated UTI. No role of routine antibiotic prophylaxis for prevention.

Emergency condition characterized by a sudden and painful inability to void voluntarily despite having a full bladder.

text:
[Acute Urinary Retention in Men | Urology | ICD-10 R33.9 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.56]
clinical_criteria:
History:
  - Nature and duration of urinary symptoms prior to AUR
  - Associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, sensory loss or weakness of lower limbs
  - Past history of retentions
  - Rule out precipitating causes: diabetes mellitus, alcohol consumption, recent surgery, UTI, constipation, cold exposure, prolonged travel, neurological conditions
  - Medication history
Examination:
  - Fever
  - Enlarged tender palpable bladder dull on percussion
  - Phimosis, meatal stenosis, urethral induration, stone, urethral discharge
  - Digital rectal examination for prostatic size, consistency, tenderness; exclude fecal impaction
  - Focused neurological examination: anal tone, perianal sensation, bulbocavernous reflex
Risk factors spontaneous bph:
  - Old age
  - Severe lower urinary tract symptoms
  - Low peak flow rate
  - High postvoid residual urine
  - Enlarged prostate or large median lobe
  - High serum PSA
  - Symptom worsening
  - Increasing PVR during medical therapy
Risk factors precipitated:
  - Surgical procedure with general or loco-regional anaesthesia
  - Bladder over-distension such as prolonged journey
  - Exposure to cold
  - Medications with sympathomimetic or anticholinergic effects, diuretics, alcohol intake
  - Faecal impaction

  - Enlarged tender palpable bladder dull on percussion
  - Phimosis, meatal stenosis, urethral induration, stone, urethral discharge
  - Digital rectal examination for prostatic size, consistency, tenderness; exclude fecal impaction
  - Focused neurological examination: anal tone, perianal sensation, bulbocavernous reflex
Risk factors spontaneous bph:
  - Old age
  - Severe lower urinary tract symptoms
  - Low peak flow rate
  - High postvoid residual urine
  - Enlarged prostate or large median lobe
  - High serum PSA
  - Symptom worsening
  - Increasing PVR during medical therapy
Risk factors precipitated:
  - Surgical procedure with general or loco-regional anaesthesia
  - Bladder over-distension such as prolonged journey
  - Exposure to cold
  - Medications with sympathomimetic or anticholinergic effects, diuretics, alcohol intake
  - Faecal impaction

clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Blood in urine, red coloured or dark coloured
  - Pain during voiding (urethra)
  - Pain in suprapubic region (bladder)
  - Pain in flank (kidney)
  - Acute retention of urine due to clots
  - Haematuria associated with clots (severe)
Examination:
  - Pulse, blood pressure
  - Check for pallor
  - Check for anasarca
  - Per abdomen examination: palpable bladder, flank mass
  - Digital rectal examination: enlarged prostate, hard nodular or smooth surfaced prostate
  - Rule out vaginal causes of bleeding
Red urine not haematuria:
  - Foods: beetroot, blackberry, rhubarb
  - Medicines: rifampicin, pyridium
Red flags:
  - Deranged kidney functions
  - Suspecting malignancy
  - Haematuria with hypertension or albuminuria
  - Persistent severe haematuria

imaging_rules:
-
  Modality: X-ray KUB
  Note: Readily available, inexpensive, minimal radiation but needs preparation, may not be preferred in emergency settings
-
  Modality: Ultrasonography
  Note: Readily available, no radiation, safe test in pregnancy, detects radiolucent stones, high sensitivity for hydronephrosis, can miss a ureteric calculus
-
  Modality: Intravenous pyelography
  Note: Anatomical and functional imaging, aids in planning surgery, high radiation, needs preparation, not useful in poor renal function
-
  Modality: CT scan
  Note: No contrast required, highly sensitive and specific, detects radiolucent stones, higher radiation and cost
-   Rule: Order X-ray KUB and ultrasound in all patients of suspected renal stones (90 percent of renal stones are radio-opaque)
-   Rule: In acute colic NCCT should be preferred if available
-   Rule: Once the stone is detected, get intravenous pyelography if stone is seen on X-ray
-   Rule: CT urography if stone is radiolucent to aid further treatment

text:
[Scrotal Swelling | Urology | ICD-10 N50.89 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.60]
clinical_criteria:
Site algorithm:
  - If able to reach above the swelling: scrotal swelling. If scrotal wall involved: parietal swelling. If scrotal wall normal and can be pinched off: intrascrotal swelling.
  - If not able to reach above the swelling: inguinoscrotal swelling
  - Intrascrotal with testis palpated separately and swelling well above testis: spermatic cord swelling
  - Intrascrotal with testis not palpable normally: testicular swelling
  - Intrascrotal with swelling just above or behind testis: epididymal swelling
Red flags:
  -
    Pattern: Painful swelling: sudden onset, tender enlarged testis, pain increases on elevating testis, severe pain, vomiting, no fever
    Suspect: Torsion testis (more common in adolescents)
    Confirm: Scrotal doppler
    Action: Attempt manual detorsion if patient reports early; refer urgently for expert consultation
  -
    Pattern: Painless solid testicular swelling
    Suspect: Testicular tumour
    Confirm: Scrotal ultrasound and serum tumor markers
    Action: Refer all cases for expert consultation

treatment:
-
  Condition: Furuncle / abscess
  Regimen: Broad spectrum antibiotic amoxycillin plus clavulanic acid; consider drainage if fluctuation or impending rupture
  Refer if:
    - Abscess appears part of underlying disease
    - Nonresponders
    - Immunocompromised patient
-
  Condition: Filarial elephantiasis
  Regimen: DEC 100 mg TDS for 20 days plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 20 days plus scrotal elevation/support
  Refer if:
    - Non responders
    - Huge size
-
  Condition: Acute epididymo-orchitis
  Regimen: If urinary tract instrumentation or dysuria, suspect bacterial and treat with antibiotic and support; refer if no response in 48 hours. Treat all other cases as filarial with DEC 100 mg TDS for 20 days plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 20 days plus anti-inflammatory.
-
  Condition: Chronic epididymo-orchitis
  Regimen: Mostly filarial. If history of UTI or urethral catheterization suspect bacterial; if history of TB suspect tuberculosis. Treat by DEC 100 mg TDS plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 20 days.
  Refer if:
    - No response to treatment
    - Epididymal abscess or local sinus discharging syrup-like pus
-
  Condition: Hydrocele
  Regimen: Small size: no treatment. Moderate to large: hydrocelectomy. Aspiration can be performed under aseptic precautions in select cases.
  Refer if:     - Not trained to do the surgery
-
  Condition: Varicocele
  Regimen: Counsel for semen analysis 2-3 times. Rest of cases given symptomatic treatment.
  Refer if:
    - Discrepancy in size of testis
    - Abnormal semen parameters present

azoospermia_algorithm:
-
  Finding: Low volume, low pH, fructose negative, retrograde ejaculation ruled out, vas not palpable
  Diagnosis: Congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens
  Next: CFTR gene mutation testing, then PESA plus ICSI
-
  Finding: Low volume, fructose negative, vas palpable
  Diagnosis: Ejaculatory duct obstruction
  Next: TRUS; if cystic seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct: TURED. If fibrous non-operable: ICSI
-
  Finding: Normal volume, fructose positive, normal FSH, turgid epididymis, normal testes
  Diagnosis: Obstructive azoospermia
  Next: Microsurgical vasoepididymal anastomosis
-
  Finding: Testes small, FSH greater than twice normal
  Diagnosis: Primary testicular failure
  Next: Bilateral multiple testicular biopsy; if sperms present cryopreserve and ICSI; if absent, donor insemination or adoption

text:
[Hysterectomy for Benign Gynaecological Conditions | Obstetrics and Gynaecology | ICD-10 not specified | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.38]
governing_rules:
- In women aged less than 40 and/or low parity it is MANDATORY to have a second opinion from a qualified gynaecologist
- Hysterectomy to be considered only when child bearing is completed and rarely in younger patients
- Ovaries should be preserved in most pre-menopausal women unless diseased or removal specifically indicated
- While doing hysterectomy for benign gynaecological conditions in pre-menopausal women, it is recommended to combine it with bilateral salpingectomy to minimise the risk of subsequent development of ovarian malignancy

[Dilatation and Curettage (D&C) | Obstetrics and Gynaecology | ICD-10 not specified | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.37]
context:
Mostly done for gynaecological indications, but may also be considered in early pregnancy complications. indications:

  - Abnormal uterine bleeding in appropriate cases

  - Infertility (to rule out TB), amenorrhoea
  - As a haemostatic measure in women with excessive or prolonged vaginal bleeding
  - Inadequate tissue obtained after office sampling
Early pregnancy complications:
  - Retained products of conception as treatment of inevitable, incomplete, missed, septic or induced abortion
  - Molar pregnancy

text:
[Postpartum Haemorrhage | Obstetrics and Gynaecology | ICD-10 O72 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.41]
initial_management:
- Call for help
- Rapid initial assessment: pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature
- Establish two IV lines with wide bore cannula (16-18 gauge)
- Draw blood for grouping and cross matching
- Start Ringer lactate or normal saline, infuse 1 L in 15-20 minutes
- Give oxygen at 6-8 L/minute by mask
- Insert indwelling catheter and connect to urobag
- Check vitals and blood loss at least every 15 minutes
- Monitor input and output
- Give injection oxytocin 10 IU IM if not given after delivery
- Start oxytocin infusion: 20 IU in 500 ml RL/NS at 40-60 drops per minute
- IV bolus of oxytocin should NOT be given

pharmacotherapy:
-
  Drug: Methyl ergometrine
  Dose: 0.2 mg IM or IV slowly
  Contraindications:
    - Hypertension
    - Severe anemia
    - Heart disease
  Repeat: Can be repeated after 15 minutes to a maximum of 5 doses (1 mg)
-
  Drug: Carboprost (PGF2 alpha)
  Dose: 250 microgram IM
  Contraindications:     - Asthma
  Repeat: Can be repeated every 20 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg)
-
  Drug: Misoprostol (PGE1)
  Dose: 800 microgram per rectal or sublingual
-
  Drug: Tranexamic acid
  Dose: 1 g slow IV
  Indication: Adjunctive treatment for PPH, used as early as possible irrespective of cause but definitely within three hours of delivery; can be repeated after 30 minutes if bleeding persists. Standard treatment for PPH must continue meanwhile.

text:
[Ante-natal Management of Normal Pregnancy | Obstetrics and Gynaecology | ICD-10 not specified | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.36]
visit_schedule:
-
  Visit: First visit
  Timing: Preferably in first trimester
  Essential tests:
    - Hemoglobin
    - Urine routine and microscopy
    - ABO and Rh grouping
  Desirable tests:
    - VDRL/RPR
    - HIV
    - HBsAg
    - WHO OGTT or DIPSI test for diagnosis of GDM
    - TSH in high risk cases (bad obstetric history, goiter, obesity or residing in iodine deficiency prone areas)
  Optional tests:     - Aneuploidy screen by USG and double marker
  Actions:
    - UPT if in doubt
    - Fill MCH protection card or ANC card, make entry on RCH portal
    - Give tab folic acid daily
    - Give first dose of tetanus toxoid
-
  Visit: Second visit
  Timing: Second trimester
  Essential tests:
    - Hemoglobin
    - Urine albumin
  Desirable tests:
    - USG Level II between 18-20 weeks for gross congenital malformations
    - WHO OGTT or DIPSI test if over 24 weeks and at least 4 weeks have elapsed after first test
  Optional tests:     - Quadruple test as per availability — should be performed only if adequate counselling facilities are available
  Actions:
    - IFA tablet once if Hb greater than 11 g percent, twice if Hb less than 11 g percent
    - Calcium carbonate 500 mg with vitamin D 250 mcg twice daily with meals
    - Calcium carbonate and IFA not to be given together
    - Single dose of albendazole 400 mg
    - Second dose tetanus toxoid at least four weeks after first
-
  Visit: Third and fourth visit
  Timing: 28-34 weeks and 36-40 weeks
  Essential tests:
    - Hemoglobin
    - Urine albumin
  Optional tests:     - USG for fetal growth and liquor
  Actions:
    - Continue IFA and calcium tablets
    - If non compliant or Hb less than 9 g percent give parenteral iron sucrose therapy (not more than 200 mg at one time and not more than 3 times a week)
    - Refer patient with Hb less than 7 g percent to higher centre
    - Refer to higher centre if any discrepancy between fundal height and period of gestation

[Asthma | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J45 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.52]
clinical_criteria:
Classic symptoms:
  - Recurrent or episodic wheezing
  - Breathlessness
  - Cough and/or chest tightness
Supportive features:
  - History of atopy, family history of asthma
  - Presence of triggers
  - Presence of rhonchi on chest auscultation
  - No alternative explanation for these symptoms
Rule out:
  - Other obstructive airway disorders (see COPD differentiation)
  - Other mimics: fever, constitutional symptoms, purulent sputum, hemoptysis, focal chest signs, foreign body aspiration, abnormal chest radiograph

control_assessment:
Period: Preceding four weeks
Inadequately controlled if any:
  - Daytime symptoms or use of rescue medication more than twice a week
  - Any night-time symptoms or awakening
  - Any limitation of activities
  - FEV1 less than 80 percent of predicted or PEF less than 80 percent of personal best
Adequately controlled if all:
  - Daytime symptoms or rescue medication twice or less in a week
  - No night-time symptoms or awakening
  - No limitation of activities
  - FEV1 greater than 80 percent of predicted or PEF greater than 80 percent of personal best

[Asthma | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J45 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.52]
treatment_ladder:
-
  Step: 1
  Trigger: Infrequent and intermittent symptoms
  Regimen: Levosalbutamol 50 microgram OR Salbutamol 100 microgram, 2 puffs SOS
-
  Step: 2
  Trigger: Regular symptoms (less than 2 per week but more than 2 per month)
  Regimen: Budesonide 100 microgram 2 puffs BD plus Levosalbutamol 50 microgram 2 puffs SOS
-
  Step: 3
  Trigger: Regular symptoms (more than 2 per week) or exacerbation in past one year
  Regimen: Formoterol/Budesonide 6/200 microgram as a single inhaler 2 puffs BD and SOS
-
  Step: 4
  Trigger: Poor control on step 3
  Regimen: Add tiotropium 9 microgram 2 puffs OD and low dose oral methylxanthine
-
  Step: 5
  Trigger: Poor control on step 4
  Regimen: Add low dose oral corticosteroids, then refer

text:
[Asthma | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J45 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.52]
guiding_principles:
- Mainstay of pharmacotherapy is inhaled drugs
- Frequency of symptoms determines treatment initiation
- Reassess at 3-4 weeks; good response is in favour of asthma diagnosis
- Patient education for compliance, warning signs, triggers, inhaler technique, PEF monitoring
- Inhaler technique to be monitored
- Follow-up at 4-12 weeks and assess disease control by clinical parameters
- Step-up or step-down treatment as per level of asthma control
- Follow up three-monthly and modulate treatment as needed
- Refer for further evaluation and management if asthma remains poorly controlled

text:
[Asthma | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J45 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.52]
exacerbation:
When to suspect: Acute symptomatic worsening, or reduction in PEF to below 80 percent of personal best, while on continued treatment
Self management:
  - Take two additional puffs of the inhaler used if symptoms persist, and repeat if needed
  - If no response after 24 hours, or symptomatic worsening, or further reduction in PEF, contact physician
Severe criteria admit:
  - Inability to complete sentences
  - Agitation
  - Use of accessory muscles
  - Respiratory rate greater than 30/min
  - Heart rate greater than 110/min
  - Pulsus paradoxus greater than 25 mm Hg
  - Silent chest
  - Room air SpO2 less than 92 percent
Severe treatment:
  - Oxygen supplementation to maintain SpO2 92-95 percent
  - Nebulized levosalbutamol/ipratropium (1.25 mg/0.5 mg) three doses at 20-minute interval, then 4-6 hourly or as needed
  - Injection hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously, then oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily for five days
  - Refer if no improvement
Discharge criteria:
  - Symptoms improve
  - Wheezing absent or significantly reduced
  - Heart rate less than 100 bpm
  - Respiratory rate less than 30/min
  - Room air SpO2 greater than 94 percent
  - Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week
Non severe treatment:
  - Manage on outpatient basis
  - Continue additional inhaler doses as needed
  - Oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily for five days
  - Schedule follow-up outpatient visit at one week
Life threatening:
  Criteria:
    - Altered sensorium
    - Orthopnea
    - Cyanosis
    - Paradoxical breathing
    - Hypotension
    - Bradycardia (heart rate less than 60 bpm)
  Action: Immediately refer to higher centre with ICU facility

text:
[Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J44.9 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.53]
clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Chronic cough
  - Progressively worsening breathlessness
Risk factors:
  - Tobacco smoking
  - Use of solid fuels for cooking
  - Occupational exposures
  - Age over 35 years
Supportive features:
  - Barrel shaped chest
  - Hyperresonant note
  - Diminished breath sounds and rhonchi
  - Forced expiratory time greater than 6 seconds
  - Features of cor pulmonale (loud P2, elevated JVP, edema) in advanced cases
Rule out:
  - Other obstructive airway disorders (asthma)
  - Pulmonary tuberculosis — sputum AFB examination in case of cough more than 2 weeks
  - Alternative diagnosis or complication: fever, hemoptysis, orthopnea, chest pain, significant weight loss, focal chest signs, abnormal chest radiograph

severity_scores:
-
  Name: mMRC breathlessness grade
  Components:
    -
      Grade: 0
      Description: I only get breathless with strenuous exercise
    -
      Grade: 1
      Description: I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
    -
      Grade: 2
      Description: On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness or have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace
    -
      Grade: 3
      Description: I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground
    -
      Grade: 4
      Description: I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing
-
  Name: COPD severity classification
  Rule: The category with the worst value should be used for severity classification
  Components:
    -
      Severity: Mild
      Fev1 percent predicted: 80 or more
      Mmrc: less than 2
      Exacerbations last year: less than 2
      Complications: No
    -
      Severity: Moderate
      Fev1 percent predicted: 50-79
      Mmrc: 2 or more
      Exacerbations last year: less than 2
      Complications: No
    -
      Severity: Severe
      Fev1 percent predicted: less than 50
      Mmrc: 2 or more
      Exacerbations last year: 2 or more
      Complications: Yes
  Complications definition: Respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, and secondary polycythemia

  - Increase in sputum volume
  - Increase in sputum purulence

  - Respiratory rate greater than 30/min
  - Heart rate greater than 110/min
  - Systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg
  - SpO2 less than 90 percent

  - Altered sensorium
  - Asterixis
  - Presence of severe co-morbid conditions such as heart failure or arrhythmia
Mild treatment:
  - Increase dose and/or frequency of levosalbutamol and/or ipratropium inhalation, or nebulized levosalbutamol/ipratropium (1.25 mg/0.5 mg) repeated as needed at 20-minute interval

  - Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days
Severe treatment:   - Treatment as under mild exacerbation plus supplemental oxygen with target SpO2 of 92 percent
Red flags refer:
  - Altered sensorium
  - SpO2 less than 88 percent despite therapy
  - Heart rate greater than 110 bpm
  - Systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg
  - High risk comorbid conditions: arrhythmia, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure
Admission criteria:
  - Severe symptoms, sudden worsening of resting dyspnea
  - Fall in oxygen saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness
  - Failure of an exacerbation to respond to initial medical management
  - Presence of serious comorbidities (heart failure, newly occurring arrhythmias)
Discharge criteria:
  - Normalization of clinical and laboratory data to pre-admission levels
  - Patient able to follow maintenance therapy
  - Completion of acute medications
  - Adequate control of comorbidities

-
  Pathway: Acute URI (respiratory catarrh)
  Findings:

    - Tachycardia
    - Pharyngitis
    - Suffusion of eyes
    - Rhinitis
    - Hoarse voice

    - Oral antihistamines (CPM 4 mg BD) for severe runny nose or sneezing

    - Antibiotics only if purulent sputum and polymorphonuclear leukocytosis
-

  Findings:
    - Fever
    - Tachycardia
    - Tachypnea
    - Crackles or bronchial breath sounds
  Investigations:
    - X-ray
    - CRB-65 score for mortality risk assessment in primary care

outpatient_cap:
Eligibility: CRB-65 score 0-1
Target organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Comorbidity check:
  - Diabetes
  - Cardiovascular disease
  - CKD
  - Chronic liver disease
  - Hepatic pathology
  - Cancer
  - Alcohol abuse
  - Antibiotics within last 3 months
Regimen without comorbidities: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS or Erythromycin 250 mg QID or Doxycycline 100 mg BD
Regimen with comorbidities: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS plus Azithromycin 500 mg OD
Duration: 5 days without comorbidities; extend to 7-10 days if no response within 3 days of starting treatment, and in patients with comorbidities
Do not give:
  - Corticosteroids unless other medical indications present
  - Fluoroquinolones as they have anti-tubercular activity
Investigations:
  Preliminary:     - Chest radiogram
  Repeat if:
    - Patient is not improving or worsening clinically
    - Suspected underlying malignancy
  Desirable:
    - Pulse oximetry in outpatients
    - Sputum microbiology in suspected pulmonary TB and non-response after 48 hours of antibiotics

text:
[Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults | Pulmonology | ICD-10 J09-J18, J00-J06, J40 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.51]
inpatient_cap:
Non icu:
  - Single agent IV beta-lactam
  - If suspected atypical pathogens, other end organ disease, diabetes, malignancy, severe CAP, or use of antibiotics in past 3 months: combination of IV beta-lactam (cefotaxime 2 g TID, ceftriaxone 1 g BD, or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 1.2 g TID) plus oral macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg OD or clarithromycin 500 mg BD)
Icu:
  - Patients without risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa: manage as non-ICU
  - Suspected P. aeruginosa (diabetes, chronic lung disease like bronchiectasis, chronic steroid therapy): IV cefepime 1 g BD, ceftazidime 2 g TID, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g QID, cefoperazone-sulbactam 1.5 g IV TID, or meropenem 1 g TID
  - Combination therapy: aminoglycosides (IV amikacin) or antipseudomonal fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin)
Adjunctive:
  - Steroids are not recommended for use in non-severe CAP
  - Non-invasive ventilation may be used in patients with CAP and acute respiratory failure
Niv contraindications:
  - Cardiorespiratory arrest
  - Presence of severe upper airway inflammation and edema
  - Severe haemodynamic instability - hypotension
  - Eu-capnic (normal PaCO2) coma
  - Multiple organ dysfunction or severe psychomotor agitation
Discharge criteria:   - Accepting orally, afebrile and hemodynamically stable for a period of at least 48 hours

clinical_criteria:
Symptoms:
  - Numbness or weakness, especially on one side of the body
  - Loss of consciousness or altered consciousness
  - Decreased vision in one or both eyes
  - Language difficulties in speaking or understanding
  - Difficulty walking, loss of balance or coordination
  - Confusion or loss of memory
  - Swallowing difficulties
  - Paralysis of any part of the body including face
  - Sudden severe headache with no known cause
  - Neck pain
  - Nausea and vomiting
Warning signs befast:
  - Balance: loss of balance or coordination
  - Eyes: sudden blurred or double vision, sudden persistent vision trouble
  - Face: deviation at the angle of the mouth
  - Arm: arm drift
  - Speech: slurred speech or inability to speak or understand
  - Time: act fast
  - Sudden new onset of headache or loss of consciousness
  - Sudden giddiness, vomiting and imbalance

  - Loss of consciousness or altered consciousness
  - Decreased vision in one or both eyes
  - Language difficulties in speaking or understanding
  - Difficulty walking, loss of balance or coordination
  - Confusion or loss of memory
  - Swallowing difficulties
  - Paralysis of any part of the body including face
  - Sudden severe headache with no known cause
  - Neck pain
  - Nausea and vomiting
Warning signs befast:
  - Balance: loss of balance or coordination
  - Eyes: sudden blurred or double vision, sudden persistent vision trouble
  - Face: deviation at the angle of the mouth
  - Arm: arm drift
  - Speech: slurred speech or inability to speak or understand
  - Time: act fast
  - Sudden new onset of headache or loss of consciousness
  - Sudden giddiness, vomiting and imbalance

[Epilepsy | Neurology | ICD-10 G40 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.34]
clinical_criteria:
Features:
  - Episodic, few seconds to minutes
  - Abnormal jerky movements
  - Loss of consciousness or awareness
  - Blank staring
  - Sudden drops, falls, brief jerks
  - With or without urine or stool incontinence, tongue bite, drooling
  - Bizarre activity out of context
  - Any other episode lasting for few minutes (usually less than 5 minutes)
Status epilepticus definition: Prolonged motor convulsion of more than 5 minutes with loss of consciousness — a medical emergency
Red flags:
  - Fever
  - Headache
  - Vomiting
  - Altered sensorium
  - Severe giddiness
  - Loss of function of body

treatment_initiation_rules:

- Differentiate between provoked seizures and epilepsy (provoked due to fever, acute CNS insult, antibiotics, and metabolic causes)

text:
[Epilepsy | Neurology | ICD-10 G40 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.34]
status_epilepticus_protocol:
-
  Stage: Impending SE
  Time: 5 minutes
  Out of hospital: Buccal or intranasal midazolam with acute repetitive seizures or status (0.3-0.5 mg/kg)
  Emergency room:
    - IV lorazepam up to 0.1 mg/kg at 2 mg/min
    - OR IV midazolam 0.1-0.2 mg/kg bolus or 0.05-0.5 mg/kg/hr in continuous IV
    - OR IV diazepam up to 0.25-0.4 mg/kg over 2-3 min
-
  Stage: Established SE
  Time: 30 minutes
  Treatment:
    - Phenytoin at 50 mg/min, 20 mg/kg, repeat plus 10 mg/kg if seizures do not stop in 15-20 min
    - If seizures not controlled or contraindication to phenytoin: intravenous valproate 25-40 mg/kg at 3-6 mg/kg/min
    - If contraindication to above two: phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV at less than 5-60 mg/min, but be prepared to intubate and ventilate
    - Second line alternatives: levetiracetam 20-30 mg/kg IV at 5 mg/kg/min (max 3 g), levetiracetam 1500-3000 mg via NGT, lacosamide 200-400 mg IV at 40-80 mg/min, topiramate 150-800 mg BID via NGT
-
  Stage: Refractory SE
  Time: 60 minutes, 2 IV drugs failed (benzodiazepine plus IV AED)
  Icu treatment:
    - IV midazolam loading 0.2 mg/kg OR continuous IV 0.05-0.5 mg/kg/hr (can go up to 2 mg/kg/hr), taper gradually after seizure stops preferably as evidenced by EEG
    - Thiopental 5-7 mg/kg IV bolus, further 50 mg until seizures controlled, 3-5 mg/kg/hr for only 48 hours
    - OR propofol IV loading 2-5 mg/kg, continuous IV 1-15 mg/kg/hr
    - OR pentobarbital IV up to 10 mg/kg at less than 0.2-0.4 mg/kg/min, continuous IV 0.5-2 mg/kg/hr
    - OR ketamine bolus 1.5 mg/kg, continuous IV 0.01-0.05 mg/kg/hr max 10 mg/kg/hr with EEG monitoring
-
  Stage: Super refractory
  Time: More than 24 hours no control

text:
[Dementia | Neurology | ICD-10 F02, F03, G30 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.33]
clinical_criteria:
Features:
  - Impaired memory
  - Anxiety
  - Hallucinations
  - Incontinence
  - Apathy
  - Aggression
  - Mood fluctuations
  - Forgetting learned activities
  - Depression
  - Sleep disturbances
  - Personality change
Important points:
  - Dementia is a complex and variable condition
  - No single test will definitively diagnose dementia
  - The clinical features if present should be a change from baseline normal functioning in a middle aged to old person
  - Assessment should aim at gathering information about changed behaviours, functional capacity, psychosocial support and medical comorbidities
  - History should be taken from a close caregiver staying with the patient for a longer duration than the appearance of symptoms
Red flags:
  - Fever
  - Rapid progression
  - Seizures
  - Recent head injury
  - Alcoholism and falls

text:
[Approach to Acute Paralysis | Neurology | ICD-10 G82, G83 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.33]
diagnostic_algorithm:
-
  Branch: Upper motor neuron signs present (brisk reflexes, extensor plantar, increased tone, sensory level, bladder or bowel incontinence)
  Likely diagnoses:
    - Acute myelopathy such as tuberculosis
    - Trauma
    - Tumor
    - Transverse myelitis
    - Epidural abscess
    - Spinal cord stroke
  Management:
    - Check pulse, BP and respiration
    - If retention of urine present then catheterize
    - Transfer or refer to nearest district hospital or medical college with MRI facility
    - Treatment will depend on MRI and other investigation
    - After treatment follow up at CHC for medications and rehabilitation
-
  Branch: No UMN signs, weakness predominantly proximal, reflexes absent
  Likely diagnoses:
    - Guillain Barre Syndrome
    - Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
  Management:
    - Check pulse, BP and respiration
    - Check serum potassium levels
    - Intubate if unable to complete sentences, single breath count low, breath holding time low, chest expansion poor
    - Transfer or refer to nearest district hospital or medical college with facility for plasma exchange or IVIg and presence of ventilator
-
  Branch: No UMN signs, weakness fatigable or extra ocular movements affected
  Likely diagnoses:
    - Myasthenia gravis
    - Snake bite
  Management:
    - Check pulse, BP and respiration
    - Intubate if unable to complete sentences, single breath count low, breath holding time low, chest expansion poor
    - Transfer to centre with facility for NCS, plasma exchange or IVIg and ventilator
-
  Branch: No sensory impairment and normal extra ocular movements
  Likely diagnoses:     - Myopathy such as polymyositis
  Management:
    - Check pulse, BP and respiration
    - Check serum electrolytes and creatine kinase
    - Transfer or refer to nearest district hospital or medical college with facility for NCS and EMG
-
  Branch: Weakness distal with lower motor neuron signs (wasting, absent reflexes, sensory impairment)
  Likely diagnoses:     - Acute onset peripheral neuropathy due to toxin or drug
  Management:
    - Transfer or refer to centre with NCS and EMG facilities
    - CSF for cells and biochemistry
    - Treatment as per diagnosis

text:
[Neuroinfections | Neurology | ICD-10 G03.9 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.34]
care_level:
Primary:
  - Check airway, breathing, circulation
  - Rule out circulatory shock, ongoing convulsions and hyperthermia (core temperature over 40.5 C) or hypothermia (under 36.5 C)
  - Establish IV access, urgent blood for hemogram, sugar, electrolytes, malaria testing (peripheral smear or rapid antigen detection)
  - Correct hypoglycemia (blood sugar 50 mg/dl) with IV 100 ml of 25 percent dextrose solution
  - If seizing: IV/IM lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg followed by loading with phenytoin 20 mg/kg at a rate of 50 mg/minute
  - When IV access not available: intranasal or buccal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg or intra rectal diazepam 0.3-0.4 mg/kg
  - Urgent referral to higher centres with intensive care facilities
Primary not recommended:
  - Stomach wash
  - Injection mannitol
  - Injection steroids
Secondary:
  - Establish and maintain airway; intubate if GCS less than 8, impaired airway reflexes, abnormal respiratory pattern, signs of raised ICP, oxygen saturation less than 92 percent despite high flow oxygen, or fluid refractory shock
  - Injection thiamine 100 mg IV
  - Stomach wash or activated charcoal if history or suspicion of drug overdose or non-corrosive poison intake
  - Start treatment for cerebral malaria: first dose IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg OR quinine 20 mg/kg bolus
  - Emergency CT or referral to centre with 24 hour CT facilities
  - Neuroimaging CT with contrast to rule out hemorrhage, infarcts, focal edema or lesions
  - Blood cultures aerobic and anaerobic
  - First dose of empirical treatment of pyogenic meningitis
  - Fundus examination and CSF study to rule out meningoencephalitis if imaging rules out mass lesions or herniations
Tertiary:
  - Neuroimaging MRI/CT with contrast to rule out abscess or herniations; if abscess, emergency neurosurgical consultation for aspiration (open or stereotactic)
  - Blood cultures aerobic and anaerobic
  - CSF analysis: biochemistry, cytology, gram staining, culture for bacterial, AFB and fungal, viral PCR, TB-PCR, fungal antigen

empirical_antibiotic:
Timing: Within 30 minutes of arrival
Regimen: If suspecting pyogenic meningitis: injection ceftriaxone 2 g plus injection vancomycin 500 mg, plus injection ampicillin 2 g if older than 50 years or immunocompromised, plus injection dexamethasone 8 mg IV
Duration: Continue empirical treatment till culture yields causative organism, then tailor treatment as per sensitivity reports for 10-14 days
Steroid rule: Steroids to be stopped after 48 hours unless any other compelling indication such as adrenal insufficiency or tuberculous meningitis

text:
[Acute Rhinosinusitis | ENT | ICD-10 J01.90 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.24]
treatment:
Phc primary:
  Duration: 7-14 days
  Regimen:
    - Oral antibiotics: amoxycillin or co-amoxyclav for 7-10 days; levofloxacin and azithromycin can be opted for patients intolerant or sensitive to penicillins
    - Topical budesonide or mometasone nasal spray once or twice a day for 2 weeks provides earlier symptomatic relief
    - Normal saline nasal washes help in clearing secretions and improve effect of topical medications
    - Topical or oral decongestant (oxymetazoline or pseudoephedrine) for 3-5 days relieves symptoms
    - Adequate hydration and steam inhalation
    - Antihistaminics in patients with co-existing allergy
Parenteral antibiotic indications:
  - Orbital or intracranial complications
  - Non-resolution of symptoms with at least 7 days of oral antibiotics
  - Worsening of symptoms while on oral antibiotics
District:
  - Surgical interventions to manage underlying anatomical conditions causing recurrent acute sinusitis such as DNS, adenoid hypertrophy, anatomical variations seen on CT
  - Ophthalmology referral for suspected intraorbital complications
  - Dental referral for suspected dental origin infection
  - Invasive fungal sinusitis: start antifungal medications, control underlying immunocompromising co-morbidity and consider debridement
Tertiary:   - Cases of acute invasive fungal sinusitis, complicated acute bacterial sinusitis and patients with immunocompromised status may be referred for management

text:
[Chronic Rhinosinusitis | ENT | ICD-10 J32.9 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.25]
treatment:
Mild moderate:
  - Address etiology and exacerbating factors
  - For allergic rhinitis, antihistamines and nasal steroid spray to be given
  - Saline nasal wash
  - Steam inhalation
  - Stretching exercises and yoga are very effective for nasal congestion
  - Topical (oxymetazoline, xylometazoline) and oral decongestants are associated with cardiovascular risks and rebound phenomenon, so careful patient selection and short course treatment to be followed
  - Intranasal steroid sprays for 6-8 weeks (fluticasone propionate, fluticasone furoate or mometasone) after discussing risk-benefit-cost issues with patient
Escalation rule: If no symptomatic relief to above treatment, perform nasal endoscopy and consider non-contrast CT of paranasal sinuses
Purulent discharge:
  - Culture directed antibiotics to be considered
  - If culture is negative, empirical antibiotics (amoxycillin, co-amoxyclav, fluoroquinolone or roxithromycin) to be given for at least 2 weeks
  - Upper dental (particularly first molar) infection may cause maxillary sinusitis which is to be treated with metronidazole
Nasal polypi:
  - Initial nasal steroid spray and subsequent endoscopic surgery is to be planned
  - Short course of oral steroid (prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 5-10 days) provides temporary relief in nasal obstruction in extensive polypi
  - Steroid therapy is not a replacement for surgery

[Epistaxis | ENT | ICD-10 R04.0 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.26]
clinical_criteria:
Examination:
  - Local examination by anterior rhinoscopy or endoscopy to look for source of bleeding
  - Little's area bleeder, clot or congestion
  - Sharp septal spur
  - Congested nasal mucosa as in URTI
  - General physical examination to evaluate cardiovascular, lower respiratory and neurological systems
Systemic assessment: Screen for coagulation disorders, anticoagulant medications, hematological malignancies
Red flags:
  - Features suggestive of neoplasia: unilateral bleeding, nasal obstruction, visual or orbital symptoms, obvious mass lesion
  - Persistent bleeding despite nasal packing
  - Altered blood counts or coagulation profile
  - Recurrent profuse bleeding: consider juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in teenage boys; aneurysmal bleeding especially following trauma to be ruled out by digital subtraction angiography; to be managed by appropriate treatment at tertiary level

text:
[Epistaxis | ENT | ICD-10 R04.0 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.26]
stepwise_management:
- Ensure patent airway and avoid aspiration by head down or lateral positioning
- Restore hemodynamic stability by intravenous fluid replacement or transfusion
- Bidigital compression of nose for 10 minutes in Trotter's position (cotton pledgets soaked in 4 percent xylocaine with adrenaline may be used)
- Short term tab labetalol will take care of uncontrolled hypertension
- Chemical or electrocauterization of bleeder in Little's area
- Tamponade of bleeders by anterior nasal packing or epistaxis balloon
- Posterior nasal packing if bleeding is not controlled with above measures
- Antibiotic prophylaxis and hospitalization is recommended after nasal packing
- H2 blockers or PPI to be given in case of blood aspiration to avoid gastritis
- Persisting bleeding despite nasal packing: consider arterial ligation (sphenopalatine or anterior ethmoidal artery)
- Selective embolization is an alternative to surgery
- Address identified etiology, if any

when_to_suspect:

- Family history of hearing loss

- Head trauma
- Recurrent or persistent (3 months or more) middle ear disease
- Chemotherapy or radiotherapy to head and neck

text:
[Hearing Impairment in Paediatric Age Group (0-12 years) | ENT | ICD-10 H90.5 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.27]
management:
Conductive hearing loss:
  - Wax removal under direct vision by ENT specialist relieves hearing impairment
  - Appropriate surgery is to be planned for tympanic membrane perforation
  - Middle ear fluid (OME) may be associated with adenotonsillar disease which needs to be treated. Initially medical treatment, and surgery to be considered for OME persisting for more than 3 months or earlier in the presence of speech and language delay
  - For non-surgical candidates or delayed surgical management, amplification by hearing aid to be reinforced in bilateral conductive hearing loss
Sensorineural hearing loss:
  - Appropriate amplification, preferential seating in classroom
  - Periodic evaluation for hearing aid users for mould fitting and amplification settings
  - Screening for developmental delay by pediatrician or psychologist

[Neck Space Infection | ENT | ICD-10 J36, J39.0, K12.2, J39.1 | overview | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.28]
Rapidly progressive bacterial infections which spread along facial planes and spaces of head and neck region. They may be fatal unless emergently treated. Most of these infections are secondary to dental infection.

text:
[Neck Space Infection | ENT | ICD-10 J36, J39.0, K12.2, J39.1 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.28]
clinical_criteria:
Presentation:
  - Acute onset of pain and swelling in the neck with fever, malaise, trismus and dysphagia
  - Extension along spaces to involve multiple deep neck spaces is frequent and may extend to parotid space, masticator space, temporal space, visceral vascular (carotid) space
  - Cervical space infection may spread inferiorly to the anterior mediastinum and posteriorly along prevertebral space
  - Tubercular cold abscess involves the same anatomical spaces but would not display inflammatory signs or rapid progression
Examination:
  - Airway assessment to rule out stridor or respiratory compromise
  - Look for signs of dehydration
  - Monitor temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, BP, and signs of sepsis or septic shock
  - Oral cavity examination to check jaw opening, condition of teeth and floor of mouth
  - Oropharyngeal examination to check for inflamed medially displaced tonsil and uvula and bulge in lateral pharyngeal wall
  - Palpation of neck for lymph nodes, cellulitis, abscess or subcutaneous crepitus
  - Cranial nerve examination to rule out lower cranial nerve palsies
Systemic assessment: Screen for diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, agranulocytosis and immunosuppressive therapy or chemotherapy. Signs of inflammation may be less marked and disease course may be more rapidly progressive in immunocompromised patients.
Red flags referral:
  - Breathing difficulty
  - Trismus
  - Torticollis or neck stiffness
  - Subcutaneous crepitus and skin discolouration or blisters suggest necrotizing fasciitis
  - Toxaemia
  - Lower cranial nerve palsy
  - Facial puffiness suggestive of venous thrombosis
  - Mediastinal extension

text:
[Neck Space Infection | ENT | ICD-10 J36, J39.0, K12.2, J39.1 | investigation | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.28]
investigations:
Essential:
  - Contrast enhanced CT scan of head and neck is the standard in evaluation of neck space infections
  - If CT scan facility is not available: lateral X-ray neck (prevertebral soft tissue thickening greater than 7 mm at the level of C2 or greater than two-thirds of the width of the vertebral body at C6 is highly suggestive of retropharyngeal abscess)
  - Ultrasound neck can suggest abscess and guide aspiration attempts
  - Blood: total and differential leukocyte count, blood sugar, urea
  - Abscess cultures with gram stain to direct antimicrobial therapy; anaerobic culture when available

text:
[Neck Space Infection | ENT | ICD-10 J36, J39.0, K12.2, J39.1 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.28]
care_level:
Phc:
  - Cautiously assess the airway; if found compromised, do endotracheal intubation or consider tracheotomy
  - Immediately gain an IV access for hydration, broad spectrum antibiotics and pain killers
  - Transfer the patient to hospital with facility for surgical drainage
District:
  - Hospitalization as an emergency for close watch and intensive management
  - Airway management: in progressive disease, in view of impending airway compromise, consider securing the airway early. During acute respiratory difficulty, tracheostomy should be done if intubation is difficult.
  - Correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance
  - Antibiotics: early and aggressive IV antibiotic therapy with a combination of crystalline penicillin, aminoglycoside and metronidazole or clindamycin is preferred
  - Incision and drainage: peritonsillar abscess is drained intraorally; all other abscesses are drained via an external approach

text:
[Otorrhoea | ENT | ICD-10 H92.10 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.29]
clinical_scenarios:
External ear:
  - Serous or purulent discharge with significant tenderness of external ear amidst edema: localized pus is furunculosis, generalized is acute otitis externa denoting Staphylococcus or Pseudomonas infection
  - Thick discharge with itching usually in hot or humid climate: otomycosis (Candida shows white spores, Aspergillus black spores)
  - Scanty serous discharge and itching with desquamated debris in ear canal: eczematous otitis externa
Middle ear:
  - URI with severe ear pain (in children manifested as inconsolable crying and ear tugging), relieved with episode of mucopurulent blood stained otorrhoea: resolving acute otitis media
  - Mucopurulent discharge more than 12 weeks: chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM). Active: otorrhoea in last 12 weeks. Inactive: no otorrhoea in last 12 weeks. Safe type: central perforation and total perforation. Unsafe type: cholesteatoma and granulation.
  - Recurrent painless profuse mucopurulent discharge with pale granulations or multiple perforations unresponsive to antibiotics: tubercular otitis media should be suspected and needs biopsy confirmation
  - Bloody otorrhoea following trauma: traumatic perforation
  - Acute onset bloody discharge with neural deficits or neck nodes: neoplasia
  - Watery otorrhoea, may be associated with trauma: CSF otorrhoea

text:
[Otorrhoea | ENT | ICD-10 H92.10 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.29]
treatment_by_diagnosis:
-
  Diagnosis: Acute otitis externa
  Regimen: Oral ciprofloxacin or amoxycillin clavulanic acid combination for 7-10 days (2 weeks maximum) and analgesics. Ichthammol glycerine (1:9) packing of external auditory canal in moderate to severe edema. Refer pus pointing furuncle to district hospital.
-
  Diagnosis: Otomycosis
  Regimen: Cleaning and clotrimazole ear drops
-
  Diagnosis: Eczematous otitis externa
  Regimen: Ciprofloxacin ear drops with steroid combination
-
  Diagnosis: Acute or resolving otitis media
  Regimen: Oral amoxicillin, erythromycin or clarithromycin for 10 days. With no response in 3 days start amoxycillin clavulanic acid combination for 10 days. Refer to district hospital if no resolution.
-
  Diagnosis: Inactive CSOM
  Regimen: Referral to district hospital for surgery
-
  Diagnosis: Active CSOM
  Regimen: Ciprofloxacin ear drops with dry mopping and referral to district hospital for surgery. A course of oral antibiotics may be prescribed in case of persistent otorrhoea after topical antibiotics.
-
  Diagnosis: Traumatic perforation
  Regimen: Topical antibiotics for otorrhoea if any and maintain ear dry till healing complete
-
  Diagnosis: Suspicion of complications
  Regimen: Start intravenous amoxycillin clavulanic acid combination and refer to district hospital

[Pharyngitis and Sore Throat | ENT | ICD-10 J02 | criteria | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.30]
clinical_criteria:
Preliminary examination:
  - Temperature chart: fever is usually absent or low-grade in viral pharyngitis
  - Check for vitals and signs of dehydration due to compromised oral intake from odynophagia
  - Complete oral and oropharyngeal examination with tongue depressor
  - Palpate for cervical and generalized lymphadenopathy
  - Rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis are potential systemic complications of streptococcal pharyngitis
  - Hepatosplenomegaly can be found in infectious mononucleosis
  - A sandpapery scarlatiniform rash may be seen in GABHS infection whereas maculopapular rashes are seen with various viral infections and with infectious mononucleosis empirically treated with penicillin
Red flags:
  - Generalized lymphadenopathy
  - Cardiac murmurs
  - Purulent productive cough with tachypnea suggestive of lower respiratory tract infection
  - Hot potato voice
  - Unilateral tonsillar enlargement
  - Tonsillar membrane going beyond its confines
  - Agranulocytosis
  - Epidemic of flu

clinical_scenarios:
- Acute onset of throat pain with or without fever, tonsillo-pharyngeal exudates, odynophagia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy is typically seen in bacterial pharyngitis; streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis is the commonest cause of bacterial pharyngitis
- Rhinitis, conjunctivitis, skin or mucosal rashes point towards a viral etiology; pharyngitis and sore throat may be the initial symptoms in epidemics of flu
- Sore throat followed by high grade fever, cough, drooling, lymphadenopathy, breathing difficulty suggest epiglottitis or laryngotracheobronchitis especially in pediatric patients
- An adherent membrane extending beyond the tonsillar confines with toxaemia suggests diphtheria
- Pharyngitis with generalized lymphadenopathy is consistent with infectious mononucleosis
- Smoking and GERD are common causes of non-infective pharyngitis

text:
[Acute Encephalitis Syndrome in Children | Paediatrics | ICD-10 G04 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.43]
management_steps:
-
  Step: 1
  Title: Rapid assessment and stabilization
  Actions:
    - Establish and maintain airway; intubate if GCS less than 8, impaired airway reflexes, abnormal respiratory pattern, signs of raised intracranial pressure, SpO2 less than 92 percent despite high flow oxygen, or fluid refractory shock
    - Ventilation, oxygenation
    - Circulation: establish IV access, take samples, fluid bolus if in circulatory failure (20 mL/kg normal saline), inotropes if required
    - Identify signs of cerebral herniation or raised ICP
    - Treat fever and hypothermia
    - Treat ongoing seizures with benzodiazepine followed by phenytoin loading
-
  Step: 2
  Title: History, examination and investigations
-
  Step: 3
  Title: Empirical treatment
  Rule: Must be started if CSF cannot be done or report will take time and patient is sick
  Actions:
    - Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 10-14 days
    - Acyclovir in all suspected sporadic viral encephalitis: 3 months to 12 years 500 mg/m2 8 hourly (minimum 21 days); over 12 years 10 mg/kg 8 hourly (14-21 days in confirmed cases)
    - Artesunate combination therapy, stop if peripheral smear and rapid diagnostic test are negative: 3 mg/kg in child under 20 kg and 2.4 mg/kg in child over 20 kg IV/IM at 0, 12 and 24 hours, followed by once daily parenteral or oral for 3-7 days
  Stopping rule: If therapy was started empirically stop acyclovir if an alternative diagnosis is confirmed, or HSV PCR of CSF is negative on two occasions 24-48 hours apart and MRI imaging is not suggestive of herpes simplex encephalitis
-
  Step: 4
  Title: Supportive care and treatment
  Actions:
    - Maintain euglycemia, hydration and control fever
    - Treat raised intracranial pressure, mild head-end elevation 15-30 degrees
    - Treat seizures; give anticonvulsant if history of seizures, GCS less than 8, or features of raised ICP
    - Steroids: pulse steroids (methylprednisolone) in children with suspected acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or autoimmune encephalitis
-
  Step: 5
  Title: Prevention or treatment of complications and rehabilitation
  Actions:
    - Physiotherapy, posture change, prevent bed sores and exposure keratitis
    - Watch for complications: aspiration pneumonia, nosocomial infections, coagulation disturbances
    - Nutrition: early feeding
    - Psychological support to patient and family

text:
[Acute Encephalitis Syndrome in Children | Paediatrics | ICD-10 G04 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.43]
raised_icp_management:
- Intubate if GCS less than 8, evidence of herniation, or irregular respirations and inability to maintain airway
- Signs of impending herniation: hyperventilate to a target PaCO2 of 30-35 mmHg
- Initial bolus of mannitol 0.25 g/kg, then 0.25 g/kg every 6 hours as per requirement up to 48 hours
- In the presence of hypotension, hypovolemia and renal failure: hypertonic (3 percent) saline preferable to mannitol, 0.1-1 mL/kg/hr by infusion; serum sodium to be targeted to 145-155 mEq/L
- Adequate sedation and analgesia
- Avoid noxious stimuli
- Administer nebulized lignocaine prior to endotracheal tube suctioning

When to suspect: Fever and two of the following: nausea, vomiting, rash, myalgia, headache, retro orbital pain, arthralgia, hemorrhagic manifestations — in a patient who lives in or has travelled to a dengue endemic area

  - Abdominal pain or tenderness
  - Persistent vomiting
  - Clinical fluid accumulation: pleural effusion, ascites
  - Mucosal bleed: melena, epistaxis, gum bleed

  - Shock (DSS): weak rapid pulse, pulse pressure less than 20 mmHg, hypotension, cold clammy skin, restlessness

  - Fluid accumulation with respiratory distress
  - Severe bleeding
  - Impaired consciousness

[Dengue Fever | Paediatrics | ICD-10 A90 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.45]
shock_management:
Compensated shock:
  Definition: Tachypnea, tachycardia, normotensive
  Protocol:
    - Ringer's lactate or normal saline 10 ml/kg/hr
    - Assess after every hour by checking HR, RR, BP, CVP and PCV
    - If improvement: RL 5-7 ml/kg for 1-2 hr, then on further improvement RL 3-5 ml/kg/hr, continue IV fluids till stable for 24 hours, then observe 24 hours and discharge if criteria fulfilled
    - If no improvement: RL 10-15 ml/kg/hr, reassess at second hour; if still no improvement RL 15 ml/kg/hr, reassess at third hour; if still no improvement colloids 10 ml/kg/hr
    - If still no improvement: look for anemia, acidosis, myocardial dysfunction and treat accordingly
Hypotensive shock:
  Definition: Tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, peripheral pulses not palpable
  Protocol:
    - 20 ml/kg crystalloid or colloid in 15 minutes
    - Assess shock by monitoring HR, RR, BP, PCV and CVP
    - If improvement: gradually decrease infusion rate — 10 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hr, 7 ml/kg for 2-3 hrs, 5 ml/kg for 2-4 hrs, 3 ml/kg for 2-4 hrs, stop at 48 hours
    - If no improvement and PCV increased: colloids 10-20 ml/kg
    - If no improvement and PCV decreased: blood transfusion
    - If still no improvement: look for blood loss, acidosis, cardiac dysfunction and treat accordingly
Referral rule: In case of shock, start bolus and arrange for urgent referral with continuous monitoring by a health professional to facilities with a PICU

text:
[Acute Diarrhea | Paediatrics | ICD-10 R19.7 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.44]
plan_a_no_dehydration:
Fluids:
  - Give extra fluids (as much as child will take) until diarrhea stops
  - Use WHO ORS after each loose stool in addition to usual fluid intake
  - Up to 2 years: 50-100 ml
  - 2 years or more: 100-200 ml
  - Frequent small sips with spoon or cup; if child vomits wait 10 minutes then continue slowly
Suitable home fluids:
  - Salted rice water
  - Salted yogurt drink
  - Vegetable or chicken soup with salt and clean water
  - Unsweetened fresh fruit juice
  - Coconut water
Unsuitable fluids:
  - Carbonated beverages
  - Commercial fruit juice
  - Sweetened tea and coffee
  - Other medicinal teas or infusions
Zinc:
  - 2-6 months: 10 mg/day for 2 weeks
  - Over 6 months: 20 mg/day for 2 weeks
Feeding:
  - Infants on breast feed to continue more frequent breast feeding than usual
  - Those not on breast feed to continue their usual milk feed or formula at least once in 3 hours
  - Give age appropriate foods to children over 6 months based on their pre-illness feeding pattern

text:
[Acute Diarrhea | Paediatrics | ICD-10 R19.7 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.44]
plan_c_severe_dehydration:
Protocol:
  - Start IV fluid immediately
  - Ideal fluid is Ringer lactate solution or normal saline (DNS in malnourished)
  - If child can drink, give ORS by mouth while the drip is set up
  - Assess heart rate, respiratory rate, BP, capillary refill time, consciousness and recognize early shock
  - Refer for hospitalization
Iv schedule:
  -
    Age: Infant under 12 months
    First 30 ml kg in: 1 hour
    Then 70 ml kg in: 5 hours
  -
    Age: Older
    First 30 ml kg in: 30 minutes
    Then 70 ml kg in: 2.5 hours
Monitoring:
  - Reassess every 15-30 minutes till a strong radial pulse is present, then every hour
  - If hydration status is not improving, give IV drip more rapidly
  - After 6 hours in infants and 3 hours in older patients, evaluate for dehydration and choose the appropriate plan
  - Give ORS about 5 ml/kg/hour as soon as the child can drink, usually after 3-4 hours in infants or 1-2 hours in children
  - Observe for 6 hours after the child has been fully rehydrated

investigation_tiers:
-
  Scenario: Less than 7 days, fever alone
  Essential: If fever less than 72 hours and child not looking sick: no investigations. If fever more than 72 hours: TLC, DLC, peripheral smear for leukocyte morphology, malarial parasite and platelet count
  Desirable:
    - Rapid antigen test for malaria
    - NS1 antigen and dengue IgM antibody
    - Blood culture
-
  Scenario: Less than 7 days with localizing symptoms
  Essential: As in first tier
  Desirable:
    - Clean-catch urine microscopy and culture
    - Chest X-ray
    - CSF analysis
  Optional:
    - C reactive protein
    - Procalcitonin
    - Ultrasonography
    - Throat or pharyngeal swab
    - Pus aspiration
-
  Scenario: Less than 7 days with non specific symptoms
  Desirable:
    - Serology for specific viral infection
    - Rapid antigen test for malaria
    - NS1 antigen and dengue IgM antibody
    - Blood culture
    - Serology for scrub typhus
-
  Scenario: More than 7 days, fever alone or without localizing symptoms
  Essential: All essential and desirable investigations from prior tiers, additionally consider Widal test
  Desirable:
    - Mantoux test
    - Ultrasonography
  Optional:
    - Ultrasonography of abdomen, chest, pericardium, joints, abscess, lymph node clusters, parotid gland for microscopy
    - Xpert MTB RIF assay
    - Mycobacterial culture
    - Bone marrow
    - ANA profile
    - HIV serology
    - Echocardiography
    - CT PET scan
-
  Scenario: More than 7 days with localizing symptoms
  Essential: All investigations mentioned in the prior tiers
  Desirable:
    - Serology for Brucella, CMV, herpes, Japanese encephalitis
    - CT scan in deep seated abscess or lung abscess
    - Bone marrow examination
    - ANA profile
    - HIV serology
    - PET scan

[Fever in Children | Paediatrics | ICD-10 R50 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.46]
management_steps:
-
  Step: 1
  Title: Initial assessment and stabilization
  Actions:
    - Decrease body temperature with paracetamol 15 mg/kg by any route and/or hydrotherapy
    - Manage any life-threatening issue
    - Consider first dose antibiotic in suspected meningitis, severe pneumonia, or severe malnutrition
    - Consider anti-malarial in suspected malaria
-
  Step: 2
  Title: Consider hospitalization for observation or management
  Criteria:
    - All neonates
    - Young infants with toxic appearance
    - Severe malnutrition, toxic appearance, inability to feed, lethargy, irritability, dehydration
    - More than 14 days illness without diagnosis
    - Any reason deemed by the treating physician
-
  Step: 3
  Title: Consider referral to tertiary care centre (after appropriate stabilization)
  Criteria:
    - Need for intensive care
    - Complex multi-system disease
    - Confirmed complications of the primary illness
-
  Step: 4
  Title: Empiric management
  Rules:
    - Consider based on likely diagnosis, sickness status and availability of investigation facilities
    - Empiric treatment should be tailored based on subsequently available investigation reports and local antimicrobial sensitivity
    - Anti tuberculosis treatment should not be started on empiric basis except in suspected tuberculous meningitis
-
  Step: 5
  Title: Consider discharge when
  Criteria:
    - Afebrile more than 48 hours or fever is showing defervescence
    - Feeding well
    - Presenting symptoms (in addition to fever) resolved or resolving
    - Physician is satisfied that further care can be continued on ambulatory basis
    - Duration of IV antibiotic therapy is completed
