clinical_criteria:
Warning symptoms:
  - Poor feeding
  - Convulsions
  - Cold or bluish peripheries
  - Stiff neck
  - Lethargy
  - Decreased urine output
  - Excessive vomiting
  - Decreased responsiveness
  - Unconsciousness
  - Stridor
  - Chest indrawing
  - Rapid or shallow breathing
Vital sign thresholds:
  - Pulse volume: high volume as well as low volume or feeble pulse
  - Heart rate and respiratory rate outside the age range
  - Capillary refilling time greater than 3 seconds
  - Pulse oximetry saturation less than 95 percent
  - Blood pressure: systolic BP less than 70 in children under 1 year; in children over 1 year systolic BP less than 70 plus (age in years times 2)
Fast pulse definition: Heart rate greater than 180 in children under 12 months; greater than 120 in children over 12 months
Poor perfusion definition: Fast pulse, cold peripheries, poor pulse volume, capillary refill time greater than 3 seconds

text:
[Sepsis and Septic Shock in Children (2-59 months) | Paediatrics | ICD-10 A41.9, R65.21 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.47]
management:
Initial:
  - Start oxygen with face mask at 4-6 L/min, or hood at 8-10 L, or nasal prongs 1-2 L/min if not available, to maintain SpO2 greater than 95 percent
  - Insert two IV cannulas
  - Give first dose of antibiotics within first one hour
Fluid protocol:
  - Give 20 ml/kg of normal saline fluid bolus over 20-30 minutes
  - Repeat bolus of 20 ml/kg over 30 minutes, with careful monitoring for hepatomegaly, oxygen saturation and crepitations in chest; if any of these appear then stop fluids
  - If there is improvement after first bolus and history of diarrhea is present: give 70 ml/kg over 5 hours in infants and over 2.5 hours in a child with hypovolemic shock; give additional fluids if losses continue
  - Start maintenance fluid in case of other illness
Inotropes: If shock persists: start injection adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and refer to higher centre. Adrenaline preparation: 0.3 times body weight in mg in 50 ml normal saline or 5 percent dextrose at 1 ml/hr gives 0.1 microgram/kg/min.
Antibiotics:
  - Over 3 months: injection ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses
  - Under 3 months: injection cefotaxime 200 mg/kg divided 6-8 hourly plus injection gentamicin 5-7.5 mg/kg single dose per day
  - If soft tissue infection: consider injection cloxacillin 200 mg/kg divided 6 hourly or injection amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 30 mg/kg/dose 8 hourly

text:
[Severe Acute Malnutrition with Complications | Paediatrics | ICD-10 E43 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.48]
stabilisation_phase:
Intake: IV fluids (DNS) 4 ml/kg/hr for 2-3 days with early or concomitant initiation of oral feeds (130 ml/kg/day)
Monitoring: Monitor vitals, urine frequency, stool and vomitus volumes
Conditions:
  -
    Condition: Hypoglycemia (RBS less than 54 mg/dL)
    Treatment: Conscious: 50 ml of 10 percent dextrose or 1 teaspoon sugar in 3 teaspoons water orally. Unconscious: 5 ml/kg of 10 percent dextrose IV. If no improvement, treat as shock.
  -
    Condition: Hypothermia (less than 35.5 C or 96 F)
    Treatment: Skin to skin care with mother in infants; warming under warmer or incandescent lamp
  -
    Condition: Electrolyte imbalance (treat empirically)
    Treatment: Potassium 3-4 mmol/kg/day orally for 2 weeks; magnesium 0.4-0.6 mmol/kg on day 1 IM followed by oral for 2 weeks
  -
    Condition: Infections (empirically)
    Treatment: Injection ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV or IM every 6 hours plus injection gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg IV or IM once daily for 7-10 days. If no response within 48 hours or critically ill, give injection ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily for 7-10 days. When accepting orally switch to oral amoxicillin 40-45 mg/kg/dose twice a day for 7 days. If prolonged diarrhea more than 7 days: metronidazole 10-12 mg/kg 8 hourly for 7-10 days.
  -
    Condition: Anemia
    Treatment: Whole blood or packed red cell transfusion 10 ml/kg over 3 hours if Hb less than 4 g/dL, or Hb 4-6.5 g/dL with respiratory distress, with close monitoring and injection furosemide 1 mg/kg at start of transfusion

rehabilitation_phase:
Transfer rule: Transfer to nutritional rehabilitation centre when child meets criteria for discharge and accepts home available foods
Feeding:
  - 6 months and above: F75 at least 5 times/day gradually increasing to give 150-200 kcal/kg/day (usually 2-3 days), then switch to F100 for next 5-7 days with introduction of home available food
  - Below 6 months: same as above with return to exclusive breastfeeding wherever possible
Micronutrients:
  - Zinc 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks orally
  - Copper 0.3 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks orally
  - Iron 3 mg/kg/day once weight gain has started, orally for 6 weeks
  - Vitamin A: over 12 months 200,000 IU; 6-12 months 100,000 IU; under 6 months 50,000 IU if food not fortified
  - Vitamin D, A, B complex at recommended dietary allowance

treatment:
Oxygen: By mask 1-2 L/min or hood 4-6 L/min to maintain oxygen saturation above 95 percent
Iv antibiotics:
  - Children 2-59 months: ampicillin 100-200 mg/kg in four divided doses plus gentamicin 5-7.5 mg/kg as single dose daily
  - Children over 5 years: ampicillin or amoxicillin, add macrolide (azithromycin or erythromycin) if atypical pneumonia is suspected
  - If suspected staphylococcal pneumonia in any age (pneumatocele on chest X-ray, post measles, infected scabies or pyoderma): add cloxacillin or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
Supportive:
  - Paracetamol for fever
  - IV fluid
  - Inhaled bronchodilators as needed
Switch to oral rule: Child is afebrile, respiratory rate has returned to below age specific cutoffs, no chest indrawing and accepting orally: switch to oral amoxicillin to complete a total of 5-7 days duration including duration of IV. If getting cloxacillin or amoxiclav, continue oral cloxacillin or amoxiclav for 2 weeks.
Antibiotic lines:
  First line: Ampicillin
  Alternate first line: First generation cephalosporins
  Second line: Amoxiclav, cefuroxime, cefotaxime or ceftriaxone

    - Difficulty in controlling alcohol use
    - Withdrawal state when alcohol use has stopped or been reduced, or use of alcohol or benzodiazepines to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms
    - Evidence of tolerance
    - Preoccupation with alcohol use
    - Alcohol use persisting despite clear evidence of harmful consequences

text:
[Anxiety Disorders | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F40, F41, F42 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.51]
care_level:
Primary:
  Psychoeducation:
    - Reassurance
    - Explain symptoms are of anxiety or fear and mimic symptoms of physical illnesses such as heart attack
    - Do not investigate excessively; few investigations like ECG or ECHO may be necessary in some patients
    - Discourage doctor shopping
    - Do not avoid triggers of panic attacks such as physical exertion or agoraphobic situations
    - Emphasize avoidance maintains fears and phobias
    - OCD: educate that the unwanted thoughts are a part of illness and not a reflection of character or hidden intentions
  Pharmacological:
    - Mild illness: spending time, reassurance and psychoeducation; may not need any medications
    - No improvement in a few weeks: escitalopram 5 mg/day at night, increase to 10 mg/day in a week. No satisfactory improvement in 4-6 weeks: may increase to 20 mg/day. If no significant improvement in another 4-6 weeks, refer to a specialist.
    - Severe and unbearable anxiety: diazepam 5-10 mg may be given at night. Do not continue for more than 1 month. Taper and stop over 2 weeks. Long-term treatment with benzodiazepines to be avoided.
    - Escitalopram to be continued for at least 1-2 years after remission
    - Monitor and address side-effects (sexual dysfunction, sedation, weight gain) periodically
Secondary:
  - Review diagnosis and treatment history if there is no improvement with a trial of escitalopram
  - Check whether the patient has taken medication at prescribed dose and on a regular basis
  - Second SSRI for about 2-3 months: sertraline up to 200 mg/day, fluoxetine up to 60 mg/day, paroxetine up to 50 mg/day, or fluvoxamine up to 300 mg/day
  - No response to second SSRI: cognitive behaviour therapy if trained therapists available
  - Refer to tertiary centre if unsatisfactory response after second SSRI and/or addition of CBT
Tertiary:
  - Evaluate reasons for treatment resistance: wrong diagnosis, inadequate drug treatment, poor adherence to treatment, inadequate CBT, presence of comorbid conditions such as personality disorders and organicity
  - Panic disorder: evaluate medical conditions that mimic panic disorder (hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, pheochromocytoma, vestibular diseases, seizures, arrhythmias)
  - OCD: trial of third SSRI or clomipramine
  - Treatment resistant OCD: inpatient treatment for intensive therapist-assisted daily CBT and for rationalization of medication regimen
  - Other anxiety disorders: trial of non-SSRIs such as venlafaxine, duloxetine, pregabalin, and tricyclic antidepressants
  - If response to medications is poor or unsatisfactory: CBT is the preferred mode of treatment alone or in combination with medications
  - Treat comorbid psychiatric disorders
  - Pharmacological augmenting strategies if antidepressants and CBT do not provide relief

  Definition: Chronic feeling of tension, apprehension, anxiety or worrying about a number of events or activities that involve everyday routine life circumstances such as work, school, health, finance, household chores

  Definition: Recurrent unexpected attacks of intense fear or anxiety along with physical symptoms such as palpitations, feelings of choking, trembling, chest pain, feeling dizzy or faint

  Definition: Marked fear and avoidance of social situations such as interaction with strangers, meeting unfamiliar people, performing in front of others
-

  Definition: Fear of going out of home alone, being in enclosed spaces such as malls or cinemas, open spaces such as bridges or vast playgrounds, using public transportation such as trains, buses or planes
-
  Name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
  Definition: Recurrent and persistent unwanted thoughts (unwanted sexual and blasphemous thoughts, fear of harming self or others, fear of contamination, doubts about daily activities) and repetitive behaviours (excessive washing or cleaning, checking, ordering)

text:
[Depression | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F32, F33 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.55]
care_level:
Primary mild:
  - Advise behavioral activation
  - Practise activity monitoring: write down activities, rate depression, schedule activities that make you feel good, make a to-do list, set clear and specific goals
  - Focus on value categories: make time for family and friends, set clear goals at work, contribute to community
  - Recommend yoga and meditation
  - Handle daily tasks: monitor sleep and diet and practise good personal hygiene
  - Supportive psychotherapy and brief counselling
  - Validate the problems and ensure frequent follow-up
  - If no improvement in 4 to 6 weeks, consider pharmacotherapy
Primary moderate severe:
  - Tab escitalopram 10-20 mg/day or cap fluoxetine 20-40 mg/day
  - Tab clonazepam 0.25-0.5 mg/day for sleep disturbance or anxiety symptoms; consider taper and stop after 2 weeks
  - If patient responds to SSRI in 2 to 4 weeks, continue treatment for 6 to 9 months and then taper and stop
Secondary:
  - Confirm diagnosis and suicide risk assessment
  - Assess for other medical comorbidities
  - Investigations: haemoglobin, thyroid function test, electrocardiogram
  - Non responder: switch over to SNRI (venlafaxine 75-150 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg) or TCA (amitriptyline 75-225 mg or imipramine 75-225 mg)
  - Cognitive behavioral therapy or problem solving therapy
  - Add on yoga therapy or meditation
Tertiary:
  - Reconfirm diagnosis
  - Assess other psychiatric comorbidities
  - Partial responder: optimise the SNRI or TCA, or augment with tab lithium 300 to 600 mg/day or tab thyroxine 25-50 microgram/day
  - Non responder: add tab sertraline 100 mg or tab bupropion 300 mg to existing venlafaxine 150 mg, tab mirtazapine 30 mg, amitriptyline 225 mg or imipramine 225 mg
  - Add on electroconvulsive therapy for catatonia or suicidality
  - Add on cognitive behavioural therapy, interpersonal therapy or problem solving therapy
  - Add on low dose antipsychotic treatment (risperidone 2-4 mg or tab olanzapine 5-10 mg) for psychotic symptoms

[Psychosis | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F20-F29 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.56]
care_level:
Wellness centers:
  - Identify, educate and refer to PHC
  - If immediate threat to self or others, refer to taluk or district center
  - Monitor and manage challenges in treatment continuation
  - If unsatisfactory outcome despite regular treatment, liaise with higher centers for optimal outcome
  - Liaise with social welfare department for disability certification and welfare benefits if continued poor outcomes
Phc:
  Initiate treatment:
    - Tab risperidone 2 mg HS for 1 week followed by 3-4 mg HS plus trihexyphenidyl 2 mg in the morning
    - Psychoeducation: medical model of psychosis, address misconceptions and build hope, inform about possible adverse effects of medications
  Follow up:
    - 2 weeks after initial contact: check for changes in symptoms and adverse effects (excess sleep, extrapyramidal symptoms, tiredness), adjust dose of risperidone and trihexyphenidyl, advise gradual return to work or school, give specific follow-up date
    - Once in 1-2 months: check for symptoms, functioning and adverse effects (EPS, weight-gain, menstrual or sexual dysfunction); adjust risperidone dose (range 2-8 mg/day) and trihexyphenidyl (range 2-6 mg/day)
Secondary:
  - Clarify diagnosis; neuroimaging if organicity is suspected
  - Negative symptoms: rule out or manage depression, anxiety and extrapyramidal symptoms; family counseling if understimulated or over-protected; consider less-sedating antipsychotics and adding SSRIs (watch for GI bleed and drug interaction)
  - Poor adherence: assessment of factors causing poor adherence and specific management; consider depot antipsychotics; liaise with primary care for assertive follow up
  - Suicidality: inpatient care, crisis management, management of comorbidity, consider ECT
  - Violence: verbal de-escalation, IV sedation, brief inpatient care
  - Assess disability and counsel about welfare benefits
Tertiary:
  - Diagnostic confusion: inpatient observation for clarification of history, thorough neurological and mental status examination, diagnostic psychometry, brain CT scan or MRI, neurology consultation and urine toxicology screen
  - Poor outcome: psychosocial interventions may be offered in isolation or in combination in inpatient, outpatient or day-boarding settings

text:
[Psychosis | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F20-F29 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.56]
antipsychotic_algorithm:
First line: Risperidone at adequate dose for 6-8 weeks to assess efficacy
Good response: Stabilization phase for 6 months at same dose. Maintenance phase: attempt to reduce dose to minimum possible dose. First episode about 2 years; more than one episode indefinite period.
Intolerable or inadequate: Choose a different antipsychotic; while choosing an alternative consider adverse effect profile and cost
Clozapine rule: Inadequate effect for 2 or more antipsychotics, after investigating for medical or neurological causes of non-response and treating them, and no cause found or poor response despite treatment of the cause
Adherence rule: At any point, if there is medication non-adherence, consider long-acting preparations in addition to other measures for managing non-adherence

text:
[Somatoform Disorder | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F45 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.57]
care_level:
Primary:
  - Detailed physical examination
  - Management of anemia and nutritional deficiencies
  - Avoid irrational use of pain medications
  - Low dose of antidepressant medications: amitriptyline 12.5 mg to 50 mg (max) night dose
  - Explain that onset of medication effect will take 2-3 weeks
  - Validate the somatic symptoms
  - Advise to engage in routine activities, physical exercise and relaxation techniques like deep breathing
  - Discuss with family members that the symptom, distress and disability are genuine
  - Strengthen supports
  - Regular follow up
Secondary:
  - Investigations to rule out any medical illnesses that might explain the symptoms
  - Complete history with behavioural observation
  - Second line medications: SSRIs (escitalopram 10-20 mg, sertraline 50-100 mg, fluoxetine 20 mg) and SNRIs (venlafaxine 75-150 mg, duloxetine 30-60 mg)
  - Combination of two psychotropic medications might be required if poor response to single medication
  - Brief counselling
  - Psycho education focusing on relationship between stress and physical symptoms
  - Relaxation training, regular exercise, yoga and meditation
Tertiary:
  - Inpatient care if needed
  - Combination of two psychotropic medications when required
  - Add on second and third line medications: duloxetine, mirtazapine, anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, pregabalin). Use of gabapentin or carbamazepine if chronic pain symptom predominates.
  - Structured cognitive behavioural therapy, cognitive restructuring, mindfulness and acceptance based approach
  - Use of alternative medicine approach: yoga
  - Collaborative approach involving physician, neurology team and pain clinic referral where indicated
  - Vocational rehabilitation if needed
  - Physical therapies: guided exercise and physiotherapy

text:
[Somatoform Disorder | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F45 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.57]
diagnostic_criteria:
A: One or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in significant disruption of daily life
B: Excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to the somatic symptoms or associated health concerns as manifested by at least one of: disproportionate and persistent thoughts about the seriousness of one's symptoms; persistently high level of anxiety about health or symptoms; excessive time and energy devoted to these symptoms or health concerns
C: Although only one somatic symptom may not be continuously present, the state of being symptomatic is persistent, typically more than 6 months. A persistent course is characterized by severe symptoms, marked impairment, and long duration (more than 6 months).
Severity:
  -
    Level: Mild
    Rule: Only one of the symptoms specified in criterion B is fulfilled
  -
    Level: Moderate
    Rule: Two or more of the symptoms specified in criterion B are fulfilled
  -
    Level: Severe
    Rule: Two or more of the symptoms specified in criterion B are fulfilled, plus there are multiple somatic symptoms or one very severe somatic symptom

text:
[Childhood Behavioral Disorders | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F90-F98 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.52]
medication_rules:
Age restriction: Avoid medication before 5 years
Severe persistent aggression:
  Drug: Tab risperidone under close supervision
  Dose: Starting dose 0.25 mg single daily morning dose after breakfast. Based on response increase by 0.25 mg weekly up to 1 mg single daily dose. Not to exceed 1 mg/day.
  Response positive: Continue 3 months followed by slow taper
  Response negative: 4 weeks trial, then refer
  Monitoring: Monitor adverse effects: weight gain, extra-pyramidal symptoms. If EPS occurs add 1 mg trihexyphenidyl OD in the morning.
Severe hyperactivity impulsivity:
  Drug: Tab clonidine
  Dose: Starting dose 25 microgram single daily dose before sleep, increase by 25 microgram weekly up to 100 microgram per day in 2-3 divided doses
  Monitoring: Monitor BP and drowsiness. Advise against sudden discontinuation.

medication_rules:
Age restriction: Avoid medication before 5 years
Severe persistent aggression:
  Drug: Tab risperidone under close supervision
  Dose: Starting dose 0.25 mg single daily morning dose after breakfast. Based on response increase by 0.25 mg weekly up to 1 mg single daily dose. Not to exceed 1 mg/day.

care_level:
Secondary:
  - Review and reassess diagnosis through detailed clinical examination using Rutter's multi-axial system
  - Review the treatment received and plan multi-modal treatment
  - Reconsider medications and augmentation strategies
  - Ascertain the presence of psychosocial factors: disturbed home environment, parent-child relationships and severe stressors
  - Screen parents for mental health problems and manage accordingly
  - Individual therapy focussing on identifying and challenging negative thoughts, anxiety management and coping with stress
  - Parent counselling to address family issues, communication and interaction patterns
  - Collaborate with school wherever necessary
  - Manage adolescents with mild or moderate suicidal risk
Tertiary:
  - Thorough diagnostic evaluation
  - Manage severe mental disorders: psychoses, recurrent mood disorders, adolescents with severe depression and treatment resistant cases, persistent suicidality, recurrent self-cutting, if necessary in inpatient setting
  - Family therapy for dysfunctional or discordant families
  - Cognitive behavior therapy for older children with severe OCD, depression and anxiety disorders
  - ECT on case to case basis: older adolescents with severe depression, mania, psychosis or catatonia unresponsive to adequate pharmacological management
  - Appropriate psycho-social steps if there is abuse, maltreatment or neglect
  - Neurology referral in suspected cases of epilepsy and organicity

clinical_presentation:
Somatic:
  - Weakness and tiredness
  - Aches and pains

  - Hyperventilation often triggered by stress or distress

  - Loss of interest in usual activities
  - Recent deterioration in school performance
  - Wanting to be alone, withdrawn, not interacting with people
  - Looks unhappy, crying for trivial or no reason, irritable, sensitive to any criticism
  - Decreased sleep, loss of appetite and weight loss
  - Talking about death and dying, self harm, or suicidal attempt
Anxiety:
  - Always worrying, tense
  - Exam tension, performance anxiety, worries about marks and ranks
  - Excessive fear and avoidance of some objects or situations
  - Reluctance or refusal to go to school
  - Very shy, avoids social situations, scared of talking or interacting with strangers
  - Clinging to mother, scared of being separated from mother

diagnosis_rule:
Persistent symptoms of emotional disturbance for several weeks, significantly affecting the child's life, unexplained by medical condition such as hypothyroidism. Depression and anxiety symptoms can co-occur. Depression is more common in adolescents and may have features similar to adult onset depression.

[Childhood Emotional Disorders | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F93 | context | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.53]
medication_rules:
Indication: Moderate case of depression or anxiety in adolescents
Drug: Tab fluoxetine
Dose: Start at 10 mg OD morning, increase to 20 mg OD after 2 weeks depending on response
Adverse effects: Behavioral activation (marked restlessness and irritability), onset of hypomanic symptoms, and worsening of suicidal ideas. Stop drug if they are troublesome.
Benzodiazepine rule: Avoid benzodiazepines except as temporary measure for a few weeks in severe anxiety attacks or panic attacks: clonazepam 0.25-1 mg/day

[Children with Developmental Problems | Psychiatry | ICD-10 F70-F89 | care_level | ICMR STW 2019 Vol 1 p.54]
care_level:
Secondary:
  - Psychological testing for intellectual disability and specific learning disorder, and diagnosis of ASD
  - Basic management of ASD: home-based parent-mediated training in social, communicative and self-help skills
  - Appropriate management of behavior problems with medication or psychosocial or behavioral intervention
  - Help parents access relevant services such as District Early Intervention Centres, parent organizations and benefits
Tertiary:
  - Evaluate and manage children with severe intellectual and developmental disability, ASD, multiple disabilities, and those with severe comorbid disorders such as ADHD, aggression, bipolar disorder and psychotic disorders
  - Investigate for the cause: review tests already done, imaging, genetic tests, metabolic tests as per requirement; arrange for genetic counselling
  - Manage treatable disorders such as hypothyroidism and inherited metabolic disorders
  - Manage comorbid physical health problems (epilepsy, visual or hearing impairment, locomotor or orthopaedic problems)
  - Assessment and management for specific learning disorder: psychoeducation of the child and parents, liaison with school, teaching basic remediation techniques to parents, issue of exemption certificates, and decisions about further schooling such as open schooling

diagnoses:
-
  Name: Intellectual disability
  Definition: Global developmental delay plus impairment compared to peers in intellectual functioning and adaptive skills
  Note: In children under 5 years, avoid diagnosis of intellectual disability; name it as global developmental delay and start intervention
-
  Name: Specific speech delay
  Definition: Only lagging in speech with normal intelligence, hearing and non-verbal communication
-
  Name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
  Definition: Marked impairment in verbal and non-verbal social interactions (being solitary or in his own world, poor response to name call and poor eye-to-eye contact) and stereotyped behaviors
-
  Name: Specific Learning Disorder
  Definition: Average intelligence with poor academic skills (reading, writing, spelling and maths) in spite of adequate schooling

assessment:
Developmental:
  - Assess if child is lagging behind in developmental attainments compared to same-age children
  - Ask mother to estimate the mental age of child
  - Ascertain if delay is global (all milestones) or restricted to one area (motor or speech)
Physical:
  - Height and weight
  - Head circumference
  - Vision and hearing
  - Any noticeable physical anomalies (club-foot) or unusual facial appearance
  - Motor abnormalities (stiffness, spasticity or weakness of limbs, unsteady gait)
  - Any other problems (heart murmurs, organomegaly)
Behavioural:
  - Hyperactive
  - Impulsive behaviors
  - Sleeping and feeding problems
  - Aggression
Emotional:
  - Excessive crying
  - Irritability
  - Shyness and fears

psychoeducation_rules:
- Normal: reassure parents
- Mild delay (at risk): early intervention and follow-up
- Explain causation due to some damage to brain before, during or after birth
- No medication can improve intelligence; teaching and training improve skills and gaining independence
- Systematic, persistent and repetitive training as per the child's ability
- Treatment of associated problems: vitamin or mineral deficiency, epilepsy, ADHD, vision or hearing issues
- Avoid overprotection, overindulgence and understimulation
